clue.text: Man following fool is given help

indicators.note: following tells us the man's name comes after the fool in the answer

parts.note: an ass is a foolish person
Ted is a man's name

explanation.surface: Someone tagging along behind an idiot gets some assistance.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone aided or supported has been helped in that way.

clue.text: When drunk, earls should be given no port

indicators.note: drunk suggests the letters of earls are reeling about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice that tipsy aristocrats should be refused a glass of port wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' signals the anagram, giving SALER. 'port' looks like the drink the earls are denied but is a harbour town in southern Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Salerno is a harbour city on Italy's west coast, an example of a seaport.

clue.text: Female Roman historian left out

indicators.note: out tells us the letter for left is dropped from the historian's name

parts.note: Livy was the historian of ancient Rome

explanation.surface: A woman Roman historian has been omitted from the record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes L from LIVY. 'Female' reads as describing the historian but is the definition: Ivy is a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivy is a girl's name, so it can stand for a woman in crossword convention.

clue.text: A number of chaps involved in craft making a book

parts.note: three is a number
chaps are men
involved in can be shortened to in
a boat is a craft on the water

explanation.surface: Several fellows aboard a vessel produce a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay also describes the plot of Jerome K. Jerome's comic novel about three friends rowing up the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerome K. Jerome's 1889 comic novel of a Thames boating holiday is a famous book.

clue.text: Rejoicing ultimately swamped by gloomy lament

indicators.note: swamped by means the final letter is engulfed inside the word for gloomy

parts.note: dire can mean gloomy or dismal

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word Rejoicing

explanation.surface: Any joy at the end is overwhelmed by a sombre song of mourning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' takes G, the last letter of Rejoicing, and 'swamped by' puts it inside DIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A funeral song of mourning is a lament.

clue.text: Spot politician in country house, maybe

indicators.note: in places the politician inside the word for a stately home

parts.note: a pile is a large stately home, a country house for instance
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Catch sight of a politician at a stately home in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' looks like a verb meaning see but is the noun for a blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: A pimple is a small blemish on the skin, a spot.

clue.text: A musical adventure which could give Randolph wet feet

indicators.note: could give tells us the answer's letters may be rearranged to produce the phrase Randolph wet feet

explanation.surface: A tale set to music that might leave a man named Randolph with soggy shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: This works backwards: the answer's letters 'could give' RANDOLPH WET FEET, so the anagram runs in reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: Prokofiev's piece for narrator and orchestra tells a children's story, a musical adventure.

clue.text: A false man misled the Anglican Church in wrongful act

indicators.note: misled suggests the letters of a false man are sent astray into a new order

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A deceitful man led the Church astray with some misdeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misled' rearranges A FALSE MAN into MALFEASAN, then CE ends it.
explanation.definitionFit: Malfeasance is legal language for wrongdoing, especially by an official.

clue.text: Girl in depression? Quite the opposite when pasta's provided

indicators.note: in would put the girl inside the dip
quite the opposite reverses the containment, so the dip goes inside the girl's name

parts.note: Lana is a girl's name
a sag is a dip or depression

explanation.surface: A sad young woman cheers up once some pasta is served.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' alone would set the girl inside the dip; 'Quite the opposite' flips the container, so the dip sits inside the name. The surface's sad girl is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasagna is a dish of flat sheets of pasta layered with sauce.

clue.text: Actor in film behind piano

indicators.note: behind tells us the film's synonym comes after the piano letter

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning soft
a film is a thin layer

explanation.surface: A performer in a movie stands behind a piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'film' looks like a movie but is a thin coating.
explanation.definitionFit: A player is a performer on stage, an actor.

clue.text: Cruel hustlers being nasty

indicators.note: being nasty suggests the letters of hustlers are behaving badly and thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Swindlers turning spiteful are heartless.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing no pity or mercy is a mark of cruelty.

clue.text: Crook making a lot of noise always

parts.note: a racket is a loud din
e'er is a poetic contraction of ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: A criminal is constantly loud.
explanation.definitionFit: A racketeer is a criminal running a dishonest scheme.

clue.text: Like some furniture with bit of damage — faded around border

parts.note: a chip is a small piece of damage

indicators.note: around tells us the word for faded encloses the word for border

parts.note: pale means faded or washed out
an end is a border or limit

explanation.surface: Antique furniture, chipped and with a faded edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' signals the container. Thomas Chippendale was an 18th-century English cabinet-maker whose name labels a furniture style.
explanation.definitionFit: Chippendale describes the elegant 18th-century style of furniture designed by Thomas Chippendale.

clue.text: Advantage held by talented gents

indicators.note: held by tells us the answer is gripped inside the words talented gents

explanation.surface: Gifted gentlemen have a lead over others.
explanation.definitionFit: An edge is a slight lead over rivals, an advantage.

clue.text: Girl, one following the fashion

indicators.note: following tells us the numeral comes after the word for fashion

parts.note: ton is an old word for the fashion or the height of style
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A girl who is one of those keeping up with trends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the ton' is a dated term for fashionable society.
explanation.definitionFit: Toni is a girl's name.

clue.text: Respond to unlikely situation with bowler coming in?

definitions.text: Respond to unlikely situation with bowler coming in?

parts.words: Respond to unlikely situation with bowler coming in?
parts.note: a promise made when sure something will not happen, pictured literally as swallowing a bowler hat

explanation.surface: Reacting to a surprising cricket development as a new bowler arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bowler' suggests cricket but is a hard felt hat; people vow to eat their hat if something unlikely comes true.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is what someone vows to do if a thing they think impossible actually happens.

clue.text: Item of clothing that creates a row, almost

indicators.note: almost means the word for row is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats

explanation.surface: A garment that causes an argument, nearly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' looks like a quarrel but is a line of seats; dropping its last letter leaves TIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A necktie is worn with a shirt, a piece of clothing.

clue.text: Remark about place, one taken as pat on the back

indicators.note: about tells us the word for remark goes around the other pieces

parts.note: a comment is a remark
PL is an abbreviation for place, as in street names
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A comment on a location, which someone took as praise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' signals the container; 'pat on the back' reads as a gesture but is figurative praise.
explanation.definitionFit: Praise given to someone is figuratively a pat on the back.

clue.text: Eat loam — strange ground food!

indicators.note: strange suggests the letters of eat loam are oddly rearranged

explanation.surface: Telling someone to eat soil, a weird meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' could be an anagram signal, but it belongs to the definition: oatmeal is oats ground down.
explanation.definitionFit: Oatmeal is oats milled into meal, a food made by grinding.

clue.text: Old devil in prison

definitions.meaning: A nickname for Satan, so the second word alone serves
British slang for a prison or police station

explanation.surface: A wicked old rogue behind bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Nick is a traditional name for the Devil, and the nick is British slang for jail.

clue.text: Salt — find it packed in box

indicators.note: packed in tells us the word it goes inside the box

parts.note: a crate is a box
taken as written

explanation.surface: Discover some salt stored in a container.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt' is a chemistry salt: a citrate is a salt of citric acid.
explanation.definitionFit: In chemistry a citrate is a compound formed from citric acid, a type of salt.

clue.text: School period — time to get stuck in

indicators.note: to get stuck in tells us the time letter is inserted into the period

parts.note: an eon is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Term time at school, when pupils must knuckle down.
explanation.walkthrough: ETON is England's famous private boarding school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College is a well-known English public school.

clue.text: Discredit a place offering a bargain?

parts.note: a bargain basement is the cut-price floor of a store

explanation.surface: Belittling a shop that offers cheap deals.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'bargain basement' is a store's lowest floor where reduced goods are sold.
explanation.definitionFit: Abasement is humiliation, a lowering in esteem, so it means disgrace or discredit.

clue.text: Distinctive scent left — but not in the nose!

parts.note: an aura can be a subtle distinctive smell

explanation.surface: A characteristic odour lingers, yet you can't smell it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: aural concerns the ear, not the nose, after a clue about smells.
explanation.definitionFit: Aural relates to hearing and the ear, so a sense experienced away from the organ of smell.

clue.text: Live to work? That gets censure

parts.note: to be is to exist or live
labour is work

explanation.surface: Living for one's job draws criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live to work' reads as a motto, but 'to' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To belabour someone is to attack them verbally, to criticise severely.

clue.text: Test gold before settlement

indicators.note: before puts the gold first in the answer

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry
a deal is an agreed settlement

explanation.surface: Assay gold before reaching an agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is the heraldic word for gold.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordeal is a severe trial, a test of endurance.

clue.text: Party entertaining upper-class couple

indicators.note: entertaining means holding, so the party encloses the upper-class letter

parts.note: a do is a party
U denotes upper-class usage in British English

explanation.surface: A party hosting a posh pair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entertaining' looks like hosting guests but means containing.
explanation.definitionFit: A duo is a pair, two people together.

clue.text: Prince's warning enthralling British

indicators.note: enthralling means holding captive, so the warning encloses the British letter

parts.note: an alert is a warning

explanation.surface: A royal's alarm captivates the British public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince's' is 'Prince is'. Prince Albert was Queen Victoria's husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert was the German-born consort of Queen Victoria, the best-known prince of that name.

clue.text: Sweetheart swallows amphibian — something you'd keep on the plate!

definitions.text: something you'd keep on the plate

indicators.note: swallows means the sweetheart takes the amphibian inside

parts.note: a lover is a sweetheart
an eft is a newt

explanation.surface: Someone's darling eats a newt, a dish best left uneaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallows' signals the container; an eft is a young newt, a word mostly seen in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Uneaten food remaining on a dish after a meal is what remains behind.
